name: Nutrition & Feeding
tagline: Wet vs dry, portions, schedules, and what a carnivore really needs.

entries.q: Is wet or dry food better for cats?
entries.a: Wet food's big advantage is water content (~75% vs ~10% in kibble) — crucial because cats have a weak thirst drive, and hydration protects against urinary and kidney problems. It's also typically higher in protein and lower in carbs. Dry food is cheaper, convenient, and works in puzzle feeders. Many vets favor wet food as the base or a mixed approach: wet for hydration, some dry for convenience. What matters most is a complete, balanced food your cat will reliably eat.

entries.q: How much should I feed my cat?
entries.a: A typical indoor adult cat needs roughly 180–250 kcal per day (about 4–5 kg of body weight), but needs vary with age, activity, and metabolism. Start from the feeding guide on the package, then adjust to keep an ideal body condition: ribs easy to feel, visible waist. As a rough guide, that's about one 5.5 oz (156 g) can plus a small amount of kibble, or ~50–70 g of dry food daily. Weigh food with a scale — "eyeballed" cups are the top cause of cat obesity.

entries.q: How often should I feed my cat?
entries.a: At least two meals a day for adults; kittens need 3–4. Cats naturally eat many small meals, so several small portions (or a timed feeder) suits them well. Scheduled meals beat free-feeding for most cats: they let you monitor appetite (a key illness signal) and prevent obesity. Free-feeding only works for the minority of cats that self-regulate.

entries.q: Can cats be vegetarian or vegan?
entries.a: No — cats are obligate carnivores. They require nutrients found naturally only in animal tissue: taurine, arachidonic acid, preformed vitamin A, and high levels of protein. Taurine deficiency causes blindness and fatal heart disease (dilated cardiomyopathy). Unlike dogs and humans, cats cannot synthesize these from plant precursors. A meat-free diet is a medical risk to a cat, regardless of the owner's dietary choices.

entries.q: Why is taurine so important for cats?
entries.a: Taurine is an amino acid cats can't synthesize in sufficient amounts and must get from animal-based food. Deficiency causes irreversible retinal degeneration (blindness), dilated cardiomyopathy (heart failure), and reproductive failure — discoveries from the 1980s that reshaped commercial cat food. All complete commercial cat foods are taurine-supplemented; deficiency today appears mainly in cats fed dog food, unbalanced homemade diets, or vegetarian diets.

entries.q: Do kittens really need kitten food?
entries.a: Yes. Kittens grow explosively and need roughly twice the energy per kilogram of adults, plus more protein, fat, calcium, and DHA for brain development. Feed a food labeled for "growth" or "all life stages" until about 12 months (18 months for large breeds like Maine Coons). Adult food fed too early can shortchange development; kitten food fed too long just adds calories.

entries.q: Should senior cats eat special food?
entries.a: It depends on the individual. "Senior" foods aren't legally standardized, but good ones offer highly digestible protein (seniors lose muscle), controlled phosphorus (kidney protection), joint supplements, and softer textures. The bigger issue: many seniors develop diseases (kidney, thyroid, diabetes) that need specific prescription diets. Base senior nutrition on bloodwork, not just age — and never restrict protein in a healthy older cat.

entries.q: Is grain-free food better for cats?
entries.a: Usually not. Grain allergies are rare in cats — most food allergies involve proteins like chicken, beef, or fish. Grain-free foods often substitute potatoes or peas, which can mean just as many carbs. Cats do best on high-protein, moderate-fat, lower-carb diets regardless of whether the carb source is grain. Choose foods on protein quality and AAFCO completeness rather than the "grain-free" label.

entries.q: Is a raw diet good for cats?
entries.a: Raw feeding is controversial. Advocates cite shinier coats and species-appropriate nutrition; veterinary organizations (AVMA, others) caution against it due to documented risks: Salmonella, Listeria, and E. coli (hazardous to cats and humans in the home), parasites, and — critically — nutritional imbalance in homemade raw diets. If you choose raw, use a commercially balanced product or a recipe formulated by a board-certified veterinary nutritionist, with strict hygiene. Never feed raw to cats in homes with immunocompromised people.

entries.q: Can I make homemade cat food?
entries.a: Possible but genuinely difficult to do safely. Studies analyzing online homemade cat food recipes found the vast majority nutritionally deficient — commonly in taurine, calcium, vitamins, and trace minerals — and deficiencies cause serious disease over months. If you want to home-cook, work from a recipe formulated for your specific cat by a board-certified veterinary nutritionist (e.g., via BalanceIT or a vet school), and follow it exactly, including supplements.

entries.q: How much water should a cat drink?
entries.a: Roughly 50 ml per kg of body weight daily (about 200–250 ml for an average cat) from all sources — and cats on wet food get most of it from their meals, so they drink visibly less. Cats on dry food must drink much more, and many don't, chronically underhydrating. Encourage drinking with fountains, wide shallow bowls (whisker-friendly), multiple stations away from food and litter, and adding water to wet food.

entries.q: Do cat water fountains actually help?
entries.a: For many cats, yes. Cats instinctively prefer running water (it reads as fresher), and fountains keep water oxygenated and filtered. Studies are mixed on average intake, but many individual cats clearly drink more from fountains — worthwhile insurance for urinary and kidney health, especially for dry-food eaters. Clean the fountain and replace filters regularly; a slimy fountain is worse than a clean bowl.

entries.q: How many treats can I give my cat?
entries.a: Treats should be no more than 10% of daily calories — for a typical cat, that's about 20–25 kcal, or just a few pieces of most commercial treats. Excess treats unbalance the diet and drive obesity. Healthy options: freeze-dried meat, small bits of plain cooked chicken, or lickable purée treats (check calories — some tubes are 15+ kcal each). Use treats strategically: training, carrier acclimation, medication time.

entries.q: How do I switch my cat to a new food?
entries.a: Transition gradually over 7–10 days: start with ~25% new food mixed into 75% old, and shift the ratio every 2–3 days. Sudden switches commonly cause vomiting, diarrhea, or food refusal. For stubborn cats, go slower, warm the new food slightly, or place new food alongside the old rather than mixed. Never starve a cat into accepting food — cats can develop fatty liver disease after just days of not eating.

entries.q: How do I know if my cat has a food allergy?
entries.a: Food allergies typically cause year-round itching (especially head and neck), overgrooming, recurrent ear infections, or chronic vomiting/diarrhea. The usual culprits are common proteins — chicken, beef, fish — not grains. The only reliable diagnosis is a strict 8–12 week elimination diet using a novel or hydrolyzed protein prescription food, with zero other foods or treats, then re-challenge. Blood and saliva "allergy tests" for food are not reliable.

entries.q: What should I feed a cat with urinary problems?
entries.a: Hydration is the cornerstone — wet food, added water, fountains. For cats with crystal or stone history, vets prescribe urinary diets that control minerals (magnesium, phosphorus) and keep urine pH in a range that dissolves or prevents struvite crystals; oxalate stones need different management. For stress-related cystitis, some prescription urinary foods include calming nutrients. Use prescription urinary diets under vet guidance — over-the-counter "urinary" foods are not equivalent.

entries.q: Are meat by-products in cat food bad?
entries.a: Not inherently. By-products are non-muscle animal parts — liver, kidneys, spleen — which are nutrient-dense and, frankly, what a cat would eat first from prey. Quality varies by manufacturer, but "by-product" on a label isn't a red flag by itself. More meaningful indicators: an AAFCO complete-and-balanced statement, a named manufacturer that employs veterinary nutritionists, and feeding-trial substantiation.

entries.q: How do I choose a good cat food?
entries.a: Look for: (1) an AAFCO (or FEDIAF in Europe) statement that the food is "complete and balanced" for your cat's life stage; (2) named animal proteins prominent in the ingredients; (3) a reputable manufacturer with nutritionists on staff and quality-control testing; (4) calorie content listed so you can portion properly. Marketing terms like "natural," "premium," and "holistic" have no regulated meaning. Your vet's recommendation outranks influencer rankings.

entries.q: What are puzzle feeders and should I use one?
entries.a: Puzzle feeders make cats work for food — rolling balls that dispense kibble, lick mats, foraging boards. They mimic natural hunting (a wild cat makes 10+ small "hunts" daily), slow down speed-eaters, fight boredom and obesity, and reduce problem behaviors. Start easy so your cat succeeds, then increase difficulty. Even a kibble scatter or a muffin tin with toys over the cups works as a starter puzzle.

entries.q: Why does my cat always act hungry?
entries.a: First rule out medical causes — hyperthyroidism, diabetes, and intestinal disease all cause genuine ravenous hunger, especially with weight loss. Otherwise it's usually learned behavior (begging works), boredom, or food that doesn't satiate (low protein, gulped too fast). Fixes: scheduled meals split into more portions, puzzle feeders, high-protein food, play instead of food for attention-seeking, and absolute consistency — one "giving in" resets the training.

entries.q: Can cats eat dog food?
entries.a: A stolen bite won't hurt, but dog food is unsafe as a diet: it lacks the taurine, arachidonic acid, preformed vitamin A, and protein levels cats require. Cats fed dog food long-term develop heart disease (dilated cardiomyopathy), blindness, and malnutrition. In multi-pet homes, feed cats in a separate room or on an elevated surface dogs can't reach.

entries.q: Is milk actually good for cats?
entries.a: No — the saucer-of-milk image is a myth. Most adult cats are lactose intolerant: they lose the lactase enzyme after weaning, so cow's milk commonly causes diarrhea, gas, and stomach upset. Milk also adds empty calories. If your cat adores it, offer lactose-free "cat milk" as an occasional treat. Kittens need their mother's milk or proper kitten milk replacer (KMR) — never cow's milk.

entries.q: Are prescription (veterinary) diets worth the cost?
entries.a: For the diseases they target, yes — they're among the most evidence-backed tools in feline medicine. Renal diets measurably extend life in kidney disease; dissolution diets can dissolve struvite stones in weeks, avoiding surgery; hydrolyzed diets diagnose and manage food allergy. They're formulated and tested far beyond regular foods, which is part of the cost. Don't substitute look-alike retail products for a prescribed diet without asking your vet.

entries.q: How do I feed multiple cats different diets?
entries.a: Separate feeding stations are essential: feed in different rooms with the door closed during meals, or use microchip-activated feeders that open only for the assigned cat. Free-feeding fails immediately in multi-cat homes — you can't track who eats what, and one cat often gets fat while another is squeezed out. Scheduled, supervised meals also let you spot appetite loss (a key illness signal) per cat.
